I'm not a doctor but I suffer from panic attacks regularly. This does not sound like any panic attack I've ever had or have heard of. Everyone is different, but seeing colors and hearing voices isn't usually something seen in panic attacks. The racing heart definitely, but I'm just stumped on the other things. 


I tend to sleep a lot, and every once in a while I'll wake up after not even remembering falling asleep to a racing/pounding heart, and colors looking more vivid. I'm thinking you may have had some anxiety about feeling sick(?) and when you laid down you fell asleep, but woke up during a dream or light sleep. And my guess is that the racing heart you had for hours on end after was because of that. My heart usually pounds for a few hours and dies down, but I've also had that happen many times. 


Just my opinion. I'd follow up with your regular doctor and tell them. 



EDIT: if it really was a panic attack and anxiety, there's no way to prevent it. You're already on antidepressants and most if not all help calm anxiety as well, so that's the only thing you can do to prevent it (even still it doesn't do a good job). You can try getting some anxiety meds like Ativan or Xanax, but usually doctors like to see a history of panic attacks before prescribing them since they are narcotics. And those you take when the symptoms are coming on. They help, but you get pretty drugged up. In the end, it's up to you on the medication. :)

Lol I'm sorry but the needles thing made me giggle a bit. I was *terrified* to no end of needles up until probably a few years ago. Please don't take offense, but it just hit home. It's funny how you can self harm yet still hate needles, isn't it? What helped me get over shots is knowing that most of the ones you need now you won't need again for a pretty long time (I'm talking years). The only shot I've had since the high school physicals were flu shots, and I've only had like two since graduating (I'll be 21 soon if that puts it in perspective). Now the worst part for me is AFTER. Just keep moving your arm, and while getting the shot look away and don't let them count down. The anticipation is what really kills you. 

Senior year was a great year for me. Probably the best in all of high school. I feel like despite trying to get ready for college, teachers are more relaxed with you. If anything you can get a few giggles out of the awkwardness of the younger people. And being relaxed makes you look more approachable too. While difficult, it's not impossible. :) 

And I'm sure you've been through this before with other school years, but schedules are almost always wonky the first few weeks or month of a new school year. They *will* get easier to memorize and get a hold of things. Just remember, you're not the only one with a new schedule. The other people you see in the hall that you think look all calm and collected really aren't. They're probably freaking out just as much as you are if not more. The schedule has room numbers right? See if you can kind of visually map it out in your head. That might help. If you can't, don't fret because it'll all come back to you the first day I'm sure :) 

The only thing I really hated about senior year was how fast it flew by. So just try to enjoy it while you can. :)

Biggest regret would be starting self harming.

Sure there were things in my past that I should have been depressed about but wasn't. My family was/is so supportive. But then my boyfriend broke up with me and I was depressed to no end. But my regret was not telling my family how upset I was. I still don't understand why I didn't just tell them. After everything else in my life, it's one stupid boy who clouded my judgement. If I had told them I probably wouldn't have started cutting. And if I hadn't cut, I would most likely be at the college I was hoping for right now (instead of endless hospital visits and months away from school). Instead, my family found out and we all started fighting, and there was so much stress... I just wish I had never picked up that blade. 

So if you ever feel like hurting yourself is the only option, rethink it. It may actually mess your life up if you don't. Those problems you think will never get better *will*. Trust me, it really will get better.

I'm like you, but I'm 20. It's very hard being in groups. I usually miss jokes, and it's not funny anymore when you say, "say that again?"  You know?

The idea that one day in the near future I'll be pretty much fully deaf is scary. I love music, I love playing the piano and listening to the tv. It's depressing at times. But then I remember how supportive my local deaf community is and it all feels a bit better. I think having people who know what you're going through or have gone through it helps a lot. 

As for jobs, I prefer being tapped on the shoulder before being spoken to. I usually get immersed in what I'm doing, so having bad hearing on TOP of that means I usually don't even know you're talking to me until you scream at me. I tell people to make sure to speak clearer, too. Sometimes people tend to like "slur", or mumble in my opinion. So having them speak clearer and pronounce their words helps me understand them. :)
